reports.text: ARCHIVE: The Israel lobby is the network of pro-Israel groups in Washington. AIPAC is the biggest one. The defense of American policy in Lebanon was always the same. America supports Israel because the American people support Israel. Jennifer Cannata, an AIPAC spokeswoman, said exactly that during the war. After denying the lobby had any influence, she said: "the American people overwhelmingly support Israel's war on terrorism and understand that we must stand by our closest ally in this time of crisis." The polls say she was wrong. On every major question Americans were closer to the rest of the world than to their own government. Who is to blame for starting it? An ABC News-Washington Post poll, August 3 to 6 2006: 46 percent said Israel and Hezbollah were equally to blame. Another 7 percent blamed Israel alone. A CBS News-New York Times poll, July 21 to 25: 46 percent blamed "both sides equally," 5 percent blamed "mostly Israel." Did Israel go too far? USA Today-Gallup, July 21 to 23: 38% disapproved of the military action Israel had taken in Lebanon. ABC News-Washington Post: 32% said Israel was using "too much force." 48 percent said Israel was "not justified in bombing Hezbollah targets located in areas where civilians may be killed or wounded." 54 percent said Israel "should do more" to avoid civilian casualties. Should America take a side? USA Today-Gallup: 65 percent said the United States should take "neither side." Zogby, August 11 to 15: 52 percent said the US should remain neutral. CBS News-New York Times: 40 percent said the US should "say or do nothing." NBC News-Wall Street Journal, July 21 to 24: 40 percent opposed "U.S. military involvement in support of Israel" if the war expanded. Should there be a cease-fire? CNN, July 19: 43 percent said "Israel should agree to a cease-fire as soon as possible." ABC News-Washington Post: 35 percent said "Israel should agree to an immediate, unconditional cease-fire." Would this hurt America? USA Today-Gallup: 44 percent were "very concerned" that events in Lebanon "will increase the likelihood of terrorism against the United States." 31 percent were somewhat concerned. ABC News-Washington Post: 35 percent said the Lebanon war would "hurt the situation for the United States in Iraq." So there was a sizable gap between what Americans thought and what their leaders did. Mass opinion cannot explain why Bush and Congress acted the way they did in the summer of 2006. Now the other excuse. Some say Israel was just doing America's bidding. A client state. Uri Avnery, the Israeli journalist, called it a war by proxy: Hezbollah is the Dobermann of Iran, and Israel is the Rottweiler of America. That does not fit either. If Israel were doing America's bidding, its bombing would have been confined to southern Lebanon and it would have protected the Lebanese government Bush had worked to install. The United States almost certainly would not have wanted to "turn the clock back in Lebanon by twenty years," as the IDF chief of staff said. Shabtai Shavit ran the Mossad from 1989 to 1996. He said: "We do what we think is best for us, and if it happens to meet America's requirements, that's just part of a relationship between two friends." Moshe Dayan said it best: "Our American friends offer us money, arms, and advice. We take the money, we take the arms, and we decline the advice." And Aaron Miller, a former State Department official, said during the war: "There is a danger in a policy in which there is no daylight whatsoever between the government of Israel and the government of the United States." whole answer to the question: The lobby says America backs Israel because Americans back Israel. But 65 percent of Americans wanted no side taken. 54 percent said Israel should do more to avoid civilians. 44 percent were very concerned it would bring more terrorism to America. The American people saw it clearly. Their government did not. And it was not because Israel was America's puppet either. Dayan said it decades ago. We take the money, we take the arms, and we decline the advice. That is the relationship. Not a partnership. Not a client. One country takes what it needs from another and does what it wants. And the lobby makes sure the money and the arms keep coming no matter what the American people say. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: American media coverage of Israel tends to be strongly biased in Israel favor. This is especially true when compared with news coverage in other democracies. The authors say this is not because Jews or pro-Israel forces control the media. They call that claim wrong and objectionable. The lobby works so hard to monitor and influence media precisely because it does not control them. Robert H. Trice did a 1976 comparison of domestic interest groups and US Middle East policy for the period 1966 to 1974. He found that "one of the most serious political handicaps of pro-Arab groups during the 1966-1974 period was their inability to gain support from any of the best-known and nationally-syndicated columnists." Trice also found that "pro-Israel groups could count on media support not only from national columnists but also from the editors of some of the country most widely read newspapers." Pro-Israel groups were more active shaping media coverage than pro-Arab groups. In 1970 for example the Conference of Presidents distributed press kits to more than 1,700 newspapers and to major wire services. The kits came with photos and feature stories. In Trice words "At virtually every level of media organization... pro-Israel groups were more successful than pro-Arab groups at getting their side of the story transmitted." But the lobby does not only shape coverage. It also attacks critics who do not obey. In August 2003 writer Ian Buruma wrote in New York Times Magazine that it is difficult to talk "critically and dispassionately" about Israel in the United States. He said "even legitimate criticism of Israel, or of Zionism, is often quickly denounced as anti-Semitism by various watchdogs." Bret Stephens was then editor of Jerusalem Post. He published a vitriolic open letter asking Buruma "Are you a Jew?" Two paragraphs later Stephens declared "What matters to me is that you say, I am a Jew." Why? Because in Stephens view "One must be at least a Jew to tell the goyim how they may or may not talk about Israel." The message was that non-Jews should talk about this subject only in ways that Jews deem acceptable. A New York Times editor also asked historian Tony Judt to identify himself as Jewish in an op-ed he had written defending the authors original London Review of Books article. ADL head Abraham Foxman told New York Times Magazine writer James Traub that it is "naïve" to think that the "free market of ideas ultimately sifts falsehood to produce truth." As Traub recounts, experience has taught Foxman that "the truth does not win on its own merits; the market for falsehood is too powerful." In this view falsehood is what would follow from a serious interrogation of the US-Israel relationship. Groups like ADL want to make sure that critics of Israel and unconditional US support for the Jewish state remain on the margins of public discourse. They want critics views about Israel to be regarded as illegitimate. So the lobby shapes what Americans read about Israel. And it attacks and labels anyone who steps out of line. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: Pro-Israel forces wield significant influence in think tanks. Think tanks play increasingly important role in shaping public debate and actual policy. News media increasingly depend on experts from Washington-based think tanks instead of government officials or academics. Most of these think tanks have energetic public relations offices designed to promote their experts views in public arena. Many also distribute brief policy memos to legislators and government officials. They organize seminars, working breakfasts, and briefings for officials and their staffs. They encourage their analysts to publish op-eds and other visible commentary. All with goal of shaping the prevailing climate of ideas. Recognizing the need for a prominent but seemingly objective voice in policy arena surrounding Israel, former AIPAC president Larry Weinberg and his wife Barbi Weinberg founded the Washington Institute for Near East Policy in 1985. AIPAC vice president and AIPAC deputy director for research Martin Indyk also helped found it. WINEP plays down its links to Israel. It claims it provides a balanced and realistic perspective on Middle East issues. But this is not the case. WINEP is funded and run by individuals who are deeply committed to advancing Israel agenda. Its board of advisers includes prominent pro-Israel figures such as Edward Luttwak, Martin Peretz, Richard Perle, James Woolsey, and Mortimer Zuckerman. It includes no one who might be thought of as favoring the perspective of any other country or group in the Near East. Many WINEP personnel are genuine scholars or experienced former officials. But they are hardly neutral observers on most Middle East issues. And there is little diversity of views within WINEP ranks. The lobby influence in think tank world extends well beyond WINEP. Over past twenty-five years pro-Israel individuals have established a commanding presence at the American Enterprise Institute, the Center for Security Policy, the Foreign Policy Research Institute, the Heritage Foundation, the Hudson Institute, the Institute for Foreign Policy Analysis, and the Jewish Institute for National Security Affairs. These think tanks are all decidedly pro-Israel. They include few, if any, critics of US support for the Jewish state. So the lobby built its own objective voice. Media and legislators then treat that voice as neutral analysis. This shapes American policy while hiding who is behind it. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: AIPAC is the main pro-Israel lobbying group in Washington. The lobby campaign to mold debate about Israel has faced its greatest difficulty in academia. Professors have tenure. Intellectual freedom is a core value on campus. And many foreign-born students and professors are more critical of Israel than Americans tend to be. So groups in the lobby did not put much effort into campus during the 1990s. The Oslo peace process was under way and there was little violence. Criticism was mild. That changed after Oslo collapsed and Ariel Sharon came to power in February 2001. Criticism rose sharply. It became especially intense in spring 2002 when Israeli forces reoccupied Palestinian-controlled areas in West Bank and used massive force against Second Intifada. The lobby moved aggressively to take back the campuses. New groups sprang up. Caravan for Democracy brought speakers from Israel. The Jewish Council for Public Affairs started advocacy training sessions for college students. A new Israel on Campus Coalition was formed to coordinate 26 different groups. Christians United for Israel formed a partnership with the David Project. David Project director Charles Jacobs said the program "will teach them how to respond so that they can say more than just God gave Israel the land. We will teach them how to understand the conflict, not as a border war, but as a regional conflict between Arabs and Jews, as the centerpiece of a global war." The most important organization was AIPAC. It had been monitoring campus activity and training young advocates since at least late 1970s. AIPAC more than tripled its spending on college programs as Israel came under fire. Jonathan Kessler was director of leadership development at AIPAC. He said the aim was "to vastly expand the number of students involved on campus, their competence, and their involvement in the national pro-Israel effort." In summer of 2003 AIPAC brought 240 college students on all-expenses-paid trips to Washington DC. They got four days of intensive advocacy training. Students were instructed to network with campus leaders of all kinds when they returned and win them over to Israel cause. In 2007 more than 1,200 students from nearly 400 colleges and universities attended AIPAC annual Policy Conference. This included 150 student body presidents. Analysis: This is the same pattern as the rest of the book. Free trips, career access, and networking are the bait. Students get training and connections. In return they become a national political machine on campus. This is not education. It is organizing for a foreign state. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # HumanRights # MiddleEast # Palestine

ARCHIVE: AIPAC is the main pro-Israel lobbying group in Washington. The lobby did not only train students. It also went after professors. In the early 1980s AIPAC recruited students to help identify professors and campus organizations that might be considered anti-Israel. The findings were published in 1984 in a book called The AIPAC College Guide: Exposing the Anti-Israel Campaign on Campus. At the same time the ADL was compiling files on individuals and organizations it considered suspect regarding Israel. It surreptitiously distributed a small booklet. The booklet contained "background information on pro-Arab sympathizers active on college campuses." It said these people "use their anti-Zionism as merely a guise for their deeply felt anti-Semitism." So the accusation was pre-loaded. Any professor who criticized Israel was labeled an antisemite hiding behind anti-Zionism. No need to look at the actual argument. This effort intensified in September 2002. Daniel Pipes established Campus Watch. It was a website that posted dossiers on suspect academics. It encouraged students to report comments or behavior that might be considered hostile to Israel. This was a transparent attempt to blacklist and intimidate scholars. It prompted a harsh reaction and Pipes later removed the dossiers. But the website still invites students to report alleged anti-Israel behavior at US colleges. My analysis is that This is the same structure as the Iraq 2003 playbook. Name a threat, skip the evidence, and force the target to prove innocence. Here the threat is antisemitism. The label does the work. A professor does not need to be antisemitic. The label alone is enough to end a career. The accusers never have to prove anything. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # Zionism # MiddleEast # Palestine

ARCHIVE: Daniel Pipes did not stop at Campus Watch. Together with Martin Kramer and Stanley Kurtz he began pushing Congress to cut or closely monitor Title VI funding. This is federal money that goes to Middle East and other area studies programs at major universities. The aim is to silence or inhibit critics of Israel and force universities to hire scholars more in line with Pipes, Kramer, and Kurtz. The International Studies in Higher Education Act (HR 3077) would have set up a government-appointed board to watch over international studies centers receiving federal money. Its mandate would include recommendations to the Secretary of Education and Congress to ensure these centers "reflect diverse perspectives and the full range of views." Sounds harmless. But this was a response to Kramer and Kurtz claims that existing Middle East studies programs were biased and fostering anti-American and anti-Israel attitudes. If the law passed universities that wanted government support would have a clear incentive to hire people who supported existing US policy and were not critical of Israel. Key groups in the lobby backed it. AIPAC, the ADL, the American Jewish Congress, and five other organizations sent a letter to Congress. The letter accused Title VI centers of "uncritically promoting a positive image of Palestinians, Arabs, and the Islamic World, while ignoring or denigrating Israel." HR 3077 passed the House but died in the Senate. A reintroduced version passed the House again in 2006 and the Senate let it expire. In 2007 Kramer and Kurtz claimed victory anyway. A congressionally mandated National Research Council study recommended a presidential appointee to oversee these programs. But the study defended the integrity of existing area studies programs and did not endorse the bias claims. Study group member Kenneth Prewitt, former Census Bureau director, said bias would be visible if it were rampant. His words: "it's not out there." The April 2007 Senate draft would create a complaint procedure. Anyone who felt a program lacked diverse views could file a grievance with the Department of Education. The Secretary would review it and "take the review of such complaints into account when determining the renewal of grants." If this becomes law lobby groups could file repeated complaints against any program that employs a critic of Israeli policy. The goal would be to cut Title VI support or push the university to tilt pro-Israel to protect its funding. My analysis is this is not about diverse views. This is about control. Use federal money as a lever so universities hire only people the lobby approves. You dont need to ban a professor. You just threaten the funding and let the university do the firing for you. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # HumanRights # MiddleEast # Palestine

ARCHIVE: In summer of 2002 pro-Israel groups at University of Chicago claimed there was "an atmosphere of intimidation and hate for Jewish students on campus." They said faculty and administrators "sanction and even encourage such outbursts." The administration investigated every claim. Only two were valid. Antisemitic graffiti in a dormitory that staff did not deal with promptly. And an email from a graduate student on a department list that told a joke about Auschwitz. That is the whole "atmosphere of hate." Still the Israeli consul general in Chicago and then the Israeli ambassador to the US visited the university. Their aim was to force the president and provost to improve Israel profile on campus. At the same time the Palestinian-American historian Rashid Khalidi, then on the Chicago faculty, had his email bombarded with spam. At Columbia the pattern was the same. When Columbia recruited Khalidi, former provost Jonathan Cole said "The complaints started flowing in from people who disagreed with the content of his political views." Edward Said, who taught at Columbia for years, said any public statement in support of the Palestinian people "will elicit hundreds of e-mails, letters, and journalistic accounts that call on us to denounce Said and to either sanction or fire him." In 2004 the David Project produced a film alleging Columbia Middle East Studies faculty were anti-Semitic and intimidating Jewish students. A faculty committee investigated and found no evidence of anti-Semitism. The only incident worth noting was that one professor may have "responded heatedly" to a student question. The committee also found the accused professors had been the target of an overt intimidation campaign. It does not stop at universities. In February 2005 Khalidi was in a lecture program for high school teachers sponsored by New York City Department of Education. The New York Sun and local politicians moved to get him fired. Chancellor Joel Klein dropped him the next day. The following year the New York City Council approved a study program on Israel "initiated by the public relations department of the Israeli Consulate in New York." A coalition of 30-plus Jewish groups also organized a national program to train high school students as Israel advocates. Philanthropists funded Israel studies chairs at NYU, Berkeley, Brandeis, and Emory. Fred Lafer of the Taub Foundation said he funded the NYU center to counter the "Arabic point of view" he thought dominated NYU Middle East programs. Sheldon Adelson proposed a multimillion-dollar gift to Georgetown. Haaretz reported a key goal was "to moderate the Arab presence at the university." Georgetown rabbi Harold White said the new center would balance the existing Arab center, which mattered because "many Georgetown graduates end up at the State Department." In every case the accusation was antisemitism. In every case the investigation found little or nothing. The Columbia committee called it an intimidation campaign. The Chicago investigation found an Auschwitz joke. My analysis is the antisemitism accusation works as a loyalty test. It moves the debate from is the criticism true to is the critic a bad person. Same structure as Iraq 2003. Name a threat, skip the evidence, force the target to prove innocence. The book gives cases where the accusation failed fact-check. That is proof it was a weapon, not a description. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Palestine # Israel # Zionist # HumanRights # MiddleEast

Keep people afraid enough and they wont ask questions. Keep critics afraid enough and they wont speak. That is not protecting Jews. That is silencing debate. ARCHIVE: Jimmy Carter made peace between Israel and Egypt. Then he wrote a book critical of the occupation. The reaction was immediate. Yossi Beilin, a prominent Israeli politician, said "There is nothing in the criticism that Carter has for Israel that has not been said by Israelis themselves." Did not matter. ADL head Abraham Foxman said "I believe he is engaging in anti-Semitism." Martin Peretz wrote that Carter "will go down in history as a Jew-hater." Carter summed it up himself: "I have been called an anti-Semite. I have been called a bigot. I have been called a plagiarist. I have been called a coward." The same thing happened to the authors of this book. The ADL called their article "a classical conspiratorial anti-Semitic analysis." Eliot Cohen wrote an op-ed in the Washington Post titled "Yes, It's Anti-Semitic." In 2007 the American Jewish Committee went after other Jews. A paper by Alvin Rosenfeld named Tony Kushner, Tony Judt, Adrienne Rich, and Richard Cohen as part of a "new anti-Semitism." Rabbi Michael Lerner of Tikkun explained what this does. Liberal Congress members tell him privately they are afraid to speak out about Israeli policy "lest they too be labeled anti-Semitic and anti-Israel. If it can happen to Jimmy Carter, a man with impeccable moral credentials, then no one is really politically safe." Even William Kristol admitted it in the Wall Street Journal. The mainstream Jewish organizations, he wrote, "have played the anti-Semitism card so often that it has been devalued." My analysis is simple. If a Nobel Peace Prize winner and other Jews get hit with this label, then the label has nothing to do with protecting Jews. It protects Israel from criticism. And people are starting to see it.
